title: Notes Receivable
description: Understand interest-bearing notes and maturity calculations.
html:
What is a note receivable?

A note receivable is a written promise from another party to pay a specified amount, usually at a specified future date.

Notes often require the borrower to pay interest.

Basic interest formula

Interest = Principal × Interest Rate × Time

Principal = amount borrowed

Interest Rate = annual interest rate

Time = portion of a year the note is outstanding

Example 1 — One-year note

A company receives a $10,000, 8%, one-year note.

$10,000 × 8% × 1 = $800 Interest

At maturity, the borrower would pay:

$10,000 Principal + $800 Interest = $10,800

Example 2 — Six-month note

Assume a company holds a $20,000, 6%, six-month note.

$20,000 × 6% × 6/12 = $600

Interest revenue for the six-month period is $600.

Recording interest

If $800 of interest has been earned and received at maturity, a simplified collection entry could include:

Accrued interest

Sometimes a reporting period ends before the note matures.

If interest has already been earned, accrual accounting may require the company to recognize that interest even though the cash has not yet been received.

Example

A $12,000 note earns 10% annually. If three months of interest have been earned:

$12,000 × 10% × 3/12 = $300

The company has earned $300 of interest during those three months.

Remember

  • Interest rates are normally stated annually.
  • Adjust the time portion for notes shorter than one year.
  • Interest may need to be accrued before cash is received.
  • Principal and interest are separate amounts.
